papers_read.title_as_printed: Identifying and Predicting Cognitive Decline Using Multi-Modal Sensor Data and Machine Learning Approach (Joshi et al., Research Square preprint, 2025)

Detecting mild cognitive impairment and dementia in older adults using naturalistic driving data and interaction-based classification from influence score (Di et al., Artificial Intelligence in Medicine 2023)

what_each_reports.P-331: 118 Nebraska drivers (72 cognitively impaired = 64 MCI + 8 dementia; 46 healthy aging). XGBoost on 3 months of naturalistic driving, wrist actigraphy sleep metrics and demographics, nested CV with leave-one-subject-out outer loop and subject-level majority vote: baseline CI vs HA accuracy 68.64%, precision 73.97%, recall 75.00%, F1 74.48%; 1-year-ahead status accuracy 70.48%. No AUC reported.
what_each_reports.P-69: LongROAD, 2977 drivers cognitively intact at enrolment, 61 later diagnosed with MCI/AD/other dementia over up to 44 months (label = most severe diagnosis during follow-up). I-score-selected time-series features of monthly driving variables plus demographics, ensemble interaction-based ResBlocks, single random test split of 90 healthy + 15 impaired: accuracy 0.96, sensitivity 1.0, specificity 0.73, F1 0.98, AUC 0.87.

quantity_a: Subject-level accuracy for classifying current cognitive impairment (MCI or dementia) vs healthy aging at baseline in a small, roughly 61:39 impaired:healthy community sample, from 3 months of driving + sleep + demographics, LOSO-CV
quantity_b: Test-set accuracy for identifying drivers who received an MCI/dementia diagnosis at any time during up to 44 months of follow-up among initially cognitively intact drivers, on a 14%-prevalence test set (15/105), from longitudinal time-series driving features + demographics, single random hold-out
incompatible_if_same: Not determinable as incompatible: accuracy depends on class prevalence; P-69's majority-class baseline is 90/105 = 85.7%, while P-331's is 72/118 = 61%. P-69's accuracy of 0.96 is 10 points above its trivial baseline, P-331's 68.64% about 8 points above its own, so the headline gap mostly reflects prevalence, not incompatible discrimination.

gates.task: mismatch: P-331 is cross-sectional classification of prevalent impairment (plus 1-year status), P-69 labels incident diagnosis over up to 44 months among initially intact drivers; registry codes P-331 T2 while the record says T1
gates.dataset_family: mismatch: Nebraska/Iowa community drivers (P-331) vs LongROAD five-site cohort (P-69); record itself has dataset_equal 'No'
gates.validation_tier: match: both internal validation (LOSO nested CV vs single random hold-out)
gates.modality_family: partial match: both naturalistic driving + demographics; P-331 adds actigraphy sleep, P-69 uses monthly time-series features over up to 44 months

endpoint_and_metric: incompatible: same nominal metric (accuracy) but on different endpoints (prevalent vs incident impairment) and very different class balance, which makes raw accuracy non-comparable
performance_validity: flag does not formally apply (0.96 < 0.97), but P-69's accuracy is inflated by an 86% majority class and a 15-case positive test set; its AUC is 0.87
independence: Distinct studies, cohorts and author groups; no shared participants
grounds: P-331 classifies current impairment at baseline in a 72:46 sample, while P-69 labels drivers by any diagnosis over up to 44 months after being cognitively intact at enrolment, so the endpoints differ.

P-69's accuracy is on a test set of 90 healthy and 15 impaired drivers, so its majority-class baseline is 85.7% against P-331's 61%, and raw accuracies across these prevalences do not measure the same quantity.
The dataset-family gate fails (Nebraska sample vs LongROAD) with no waiver on record, and the predictor sets differ (sleep actigraphy vs 44-month time-series features).

evidence_quotes.quote: this group combined with those classified as MCI (N = 64) to form a single unified cognitive impairment group (N = 72). The remaining participants (N = 46) were classified as the healthy aging.
the model 6 integrating demographics, driving performance, driving life-space, and sleep data achieved the highest accuracy (68.64%), precision (73.97%), and F1-score (74.48%).
Naturalistic driving trajectories were collected through in-vehicle recording devices for up to 44 months from 2977 participants who were cognitively intact at the time of enrollment.

However, here we only use the most severe one. For instance, if one participant was healthy at the beginning of the study but gradually moved to MCI, unspecified dementia, and then Alzheimer's disease, we will assign a value of one for this participant.
We randomly select 90 healthy and 15 dementia data points as the test data, and use the remaining 2826 healthy and 46 dementia data points as the training data.
our proposed classification method achieves the best accuracy (96%) for predicting MCI and dementia, followed by random forest (93%) and logistic regression (88%).

record_defects: claim_a 'P-331: Acc 68.64 on T1': registry codes P-331 as T2 and the paper reports both baseline classification and 1-year prediction.
resolution_note asserts 'Confirmed genuine: Same metric type (Acc)' without accounting for the different prevalence (P-69 test set 15/105 impaired) and endpoints.
Registry Best_Metric for P-69 is 'AUC 0.87' while the record claims '96% Acc'; both are in the paper, but the record chose the prevalence-sensitive metric.
Bridging list contains precision and AUC values described as comparable to an accuracy gap.
what_would_change_the_verdict: Both studies reporting a prevalence-robust metric (AUC or balanced accuracy) for the same endpoint (e.g. prevalent MCI/dementia vs healthy) in comparable driving cohorts.
